title: A Lie, a Prison, a Warning
overview: The young Jesus movement in Jerusalem faces trouble from a dishonest couple inside it and from the temple leaders outside it, yet it keeps growing.

parts.label: Ananias and Sapphira lie (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Like others before them, this couple sold land to support the group, but they kept some of the money while presenting the rest as the full price. Peter says the land and the money were always theirs to keep, so the wrong was the pretending, not the keeping.

parts.label: Two sudden deaths (vv. 5-11)
parts.note: Each falls dead when confronted, and the story presents this as God's judgment, leaving the whole community afraid. It is a stark, unsettling account, and readers through the centuries have found it hard to sit with.

parts.label: Healing in the temple area (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: Solomon's Colonnade was a long covered walkway along the temple courts where the believers gathered. People hoped even Peter's passing shadow might heal their sick, which shows how far his reputation had spread.

parts.label: Arrested and set free (vv. 17-26)
parts.note: The Sadducees, a priestly group who ran the temple and rejected belief in resurrection, jailed the apostles, but the text says an angel freed them overnight and they went straight back to teaching. The officers brought them in without force because they feared the crowd would stone them.

parts.label: Before the council (vv. 27-32)
parts.note: The Sanhedrin, Jerusalem's highest Jewish council, had banned their preaching and objected to being blamed for Jesus' death. Peter answers that they must obey God rather than people, and says God raised Jesus to bring Israel to repentance and forgive their sins.

parts.label: Gamaliel's advice and release (vv. 33-42)
parts.note: Gamaliel, a respected teacher of the law, argued that merely human movements fade on their own, so fighting this one could mean fighting God (scholars debate the dating of his example, Theudas). The apostles were whipped and released, and they treated the disgrace as an honor while they kept on teaching.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira, some seeing a unique judgment tied to the church's beginnings and others asking what, if anything, it says about how God deals with dishonesty today.
think: What makes people want to look more generous or committed than they really are?
